cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Who Changed It?
cards.instruction: Ask innocent questions until someone admits altering the plan, schedule, arrangement, or shared space.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. I can't open the cupboard. Was the sofa this close yesterday?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: There's more room for yoga now.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. Did making that room involve moving the sofa?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Yes, I moved it. I put the things you'll need somewhere easier.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: How thoughtful. Would those be the mugs in your sock drawer, or has someone else improved the kitchen too?

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 decides and A3 restricts questions, but A5 ironic mug question does not clearly retain approval over B helpful rearrangement.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 yoga space causes A3 sofa-move question; B4 admission and item relocation cause A5 mug-location probe, after an unrelated restriction.

relationship.evidence: B2 explains a practical aim and B4 admits while offering helpful intent, making the changes more than arbitrary vandalism.

heightening.evidence: B4 sofa confession opens a further admission about moved kitchen items at A5.

specificity.evidence: A1 blocked cupboard, B2 yoga and A5 mugs in a sock drawer give concrete shared-space consequences.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 someone-else-improved-the-kitchen follows B4 helpful claim; the generic A3 authority preface is clumsy.
